title: ⭐ Practice: the tools of the language

questions.prompt: Match each reference book with what it gives you.

options.text: A dictionary of synonyms and antonyms
The meaning of a word, in the same language or in another one
Words of similar meaning, with their opposites printed underneath
An exhaustive list of equivalents, arranged in groups according to sense
Information about many subjects, arranged in alphabetical order

questions.explanation: A dictionary tells you what a word means, in the same language or in another one. A dictionary of synonyms and antonyms prints both lists together: under talented you read able, gifted, clever and adept, then, on its own line, the antonyms clumsy and inept. A thesaurus collects words in groups according to sense and hands you the exhaustive list of equivalents — a whole column for tale where a dictionary gives one line. An encyclopedia leaves words aside altogether and describes subjects, in alphabetical order. Ask yourself what you actually need — a meaning, an opposite, a better word or a fact — and the book chooses itself.

questions.prompt: Colloquial English contrasts with formal English. Where would you normally hear it?
questions.explanation: Colloquial English is the English of everyday conversations: relaxed, spoken, full of short forms such as cuppa for a cup of tea. Lectures, essays and official reports all call for formal English, the variety a dictionary marks as neutral or formal. Choosing the wrong one is not a grammar mistake, it is a mistake of register — and an examiner notices it immediately.

questions.prompt: Three of these words form a strong partnership with the adjective NEW. Which one does not?
questions.explanation: English has a new style, a new situation and a new look, but never "a new someone" — with a person you say somebody new, or a new friend. There is no rule and no logical explanation behind a partnership of this kind: words that occur together frequently collocate, and words that do not sound unnatural and wrong even when each of them is perfectly correct on its own.

questions.prompt: Check ALL the combinations that English speakers really use.
questions.explanation: English fixes these partnerships by usage, not by logic: you make a phone call, you make an effort, and you do the shopping. The two that never occur are built the other way round — English says make a mistake, and it says do your homework. Do and make cannot be exchanged, nothing in their meaning predicts which noun takes which verb, and that is why every pair has to be learnt as a single block rather than translated from Arabic or French.

questions.prompt: Your neighbour is carrying a heavy suitcase up the stairs and says: "Give me a hand, will you?" What is he asking for?
questions.explanation: To give somebody a hand means to help or to assist them, so your neighbour wants you to take one end of the suitcase. Every word in the phrase is easy, yet together they say something none of them says alone — that is exactly what an idiomatic expression is. A handshake and a wave read hand literally, and to give somebody a big hand does mean to applaud, but nobody applauds a suitcase on the stairs.

questions.prompt: "Our neighbour walked to the theatre." How would an American write this sentence?

options.text: Our neighbour walked to the theater.
Our neighbor walked to the theatre.
Our neighbor walked to the theater.
Our neighbour walked to the theatre.

questions.explanation: American English drops the u of the British -our ending — neighbour becomes neighbor, humour becomes humor, honour becomes honor — and it turns the British -re ending round: theatre becomes theater, centre becomes center, metre becomes meter. Both changes apply in this sentence, so both words are respelt; leaving the sentence exactly as it stands keeps it British, and changing only one of the two words makes it half British and half American, which is the one thing no variety allows.
